q: Match List I (psychologist) with List II (theory): A. Dollard and Miller, B. Skinner, C. Bandura and Walters, D. Maslow; 1. Radical behaviorism, 2. Self-actualization, 3. Early social learning, 4. Later social learning.
who: Dollard and Miller (1950); Bandura and Walters (1963)

concept.t: Dollard and Miller translated Freud into Hull's learning terms in 1950; this is the early social learning theory.
Bandura and Walters gave the later social learning theory in 1963.
Skinner's system is radical behaviourism, and Maslow is self-actualisation.

wrong.a: Gets every pair wrong: Dollard and Miller are not radical behaviourists, Skinner is not self-actualisation, Bandura and Walters are the later theory, and Maslow is not social learning.
wrong.c: Only B-1 is right: Dollard and Miller get self-actualisation, Bandura and Walters the early theory, and Maslow the later social learning theory.
wrong.d: Tempting because A-3 and C-4 are right, but it swaps Skinner and Maslow: Skinner, not Maslow, is the radical behaviourist.

q: Psychology studies both overt and covert behaviour. Covert behaviour is:

concept.t: Covert (implicit) behaviour cannot be seen by an observer but can be measured with instruments.
Watson's subvocal speech is covert: you cannot see it, but instruments can record it.
Overt behaviour is both observable and measurable.

wrong.a: Describes overt behaviour, the wrong kind: overt behaviour is both observable and measurable.
wrong.c: Says much the same as (b) but less precisely, since it drops the key point that covert behaviour cannot be observed.
wrong.d: The reverse of the truth: covert behaviour is exactly the kind an observer cannot see.

q: Latent learning was demonstrated by:

concept.t: Tolman and Honzik (1930) let rats run a maze with no reward; they learned it but did not show it.
When food appeared, the rats revealed the learning at once. Learning had been latent, evidence for a cognitive map.

wrong.b: Bandura is observational learning, learning by watching others, not hidden maze learning.
wrong.c: Skinner is operant conditioning, learning through reward; Tolman's point was that rats learned without any reward.
wrong.d: Kohler is insight learning, the sudden solution of a problem, shown in his work with chimpanzees.

q: Gestalt psychology emphasizes:

concept.t: "The whole is greater than the sum of its parts" is the Gestalt school's slogan: we perceive organised wholes, not piles of separate sensations.
Koffka preferred "different from" the sum of its parts, because the whole is a new thing, not just more.

wrong.a: Behaviourist ideas about how consequences shape behaviour, not Gestalt.
wrong.b: Belong to the biological perspective, not to the Gestalt school.
wrong.c: Belong to Beck's cognitive therapy, not to the Gestalt school.

q: In Lewin's topological system, emphasis was placed on the study of 'life space,' which includes:
who: Kurt Lewin, field theory: B = f(P, E)

concept.t: The life space is the person plus the environment as it exists for that person.
Hence B = f(P, E): behaviour is a function of the person and the psychological environment.
Groups were a later application of field theory (group dynamics), not part of the definition of the life space.

wrong.b: Leaves out the person entirely; groups were a later application of field theory (group dynamics), not part of the life space.
wrong.c: Keeps the person but swaps the psychological environment for the group, which belongs to the later group dynamics work.
wrong.d: Drops the person, half of B = f(P, E), and adds the group, a later application of field theory.

q: Kurt Lewin is widely titled the father of modern social psychology. Which OTHER field is he also credited with founding?
who: Kurt Lewin, founder of action research

concept.t: Action research is a cycle of planning, acting, observing and reflecting.
It is done with the people affected, not on them. Lewin founded it.

wrong.a: Freud's creation, not Lewin's.
wrong.c: Fechner's field, not Lewin's.
wrong.d: Belongs to James, Dewey and Angell, not Lewin.

q: Which therapy focuses on "empty chair technique"?

concept.t: In the empty chair, the client holds a dialogue with an absent person or a disowned part of the self.
It is Fritz Perls's technique, a signature of Gestalt therapy.
Gestalt therapy is Perls's; it is not the Gestalt psychology of Wertheimer, Kohler and Koffka.

wrong.a: Does not use the empty chair as a signature technique.
wrong.c: Freud's method, built on free association; it does not use the empty chair as a signature technique.
wrong.d: Linehan's skills-based therapy, which does not use the empty chair as a signature technique.

q: Which perspective in psychology emphasizes unconscious processes and early childhood experiences?

concept.t: The psychodynamic perspective, descended from Freud, explains behaviour by unconscious conflict.
It also stresses early experience, the second cue in the stem; no other perspective here (behavioural, humanistic, cognitive) centres on both.

wrong.a: Stresses conditioning, not unconscious conflict or childhood.
wrong.c: Stresses free will and growth, not unconscious conflict.
wrong.d: Stresses internal mental processes, not unconscious conflict or childhood.

q: Noogenic anxiety is described under:

concept.t: Frankl's noogenic neurosis (and anxiety) arises from frustrated meaning.
Meaning belongs to the spiritual dimension, which places the concept in existential psychology.
The humanistic school is a close neighbour, but the concept is Frankl's, not Maslow's or Rogers's.

wrong.a: A close neighbour, but noogenic anxiety is Frankl's concept, not Maslow's or Rogers's.
wrong.b: The Gestalt school studied perception and organised wholes; it has no concept of anxiety from frustrated meaning.
wrong.d: Freud's school explains anxiety by unconscious conflict, not by frustrated meaning.

q: The concept of "Dasein," which refers to human existence as "being-in-the-world," is primarily associated with which school of psychology?

concept.t: Dasein is Heidegger's term for human existence as being-in-the-world (Being and Time, 1927).
Binswanger and Boss made it clinical in Daseinsanalysis, a form of existential psychology.

wrong.a: Does not use the term Dasein; it studies observable behaviour.
wrong.c: Does not use the term Dasein; it studies mental processes such as memory and thinking.
wrong.d: Freud's school of the unconscious; it does not use the term Dasein.

q: Viktor Frankl's concept of the "will to meaning," the fundamental motivational force in humans to find purpose in life, is central to which therapeutic school?

concept.t: Logotherapy is Frankl's own school, the "third Viennese school" (after Freud's and Adler's), and it rests on the will to meaning.
Existential-humanistic therapy is the broad family logotherapy belongs to; choose the most specific answer.

wrong.a: Ellis's therapy, not Frankl's.
wrong.c: The broad family logotherapy belongs to, so it is the tempting but less specific answer.
wrong.d: Hayes's therapy, not Frankl's.

q: Savoring is a concept in Positive Psychology that involves:

concept.t: Bryant and Veroff defined savouring as attending to, appreciating and intensifying positive experiences.
It covers positive experiences past, present or anticipated.
Savouring is to good events what coping is to bad ones.

wrong.a: Describes avoidance; savouring moves towards good experiences rather than away from bad ones.
wrong.c: Describes relaxation; savouring is about enjoyment, not stress control.
wrong.d: Describes trauma work; savouring deals with positive, not painful, experiences.

q: Who is a pioneer contributor to Cognitive Psychology?
who: Jean Piaget, studies of thinking from the 1920s

concept.t: Piaget studied the growth of thinking from the 1920s, long before the cognitive revolution.
So he is treated as a forerunner of cognitive psychology.

wrong.b: A Gestalt psychologist, not a cognitive pioneer.
wrong.c: A linguist whose 1959 review fuelled the cognitive revolution; tempting, but that came decades after Piaget began.
wrong.d: A theorist of moral development, not a pioneer of cognitive psychology.

q: "Third-wave CBT" includes all EXCEPT:
who: Third wave of CBT (acceptance and mindfulness therapies)

concept.t: The third wave comprises acceptance and mindfulness-based therapies, many drawing on Buddhist practice.
The first wave was behaviour therapy and the second was cognitive therapy.
Psychoanalysis is the first force in psychology and is not a wave of CBT at all.

wrong.a: True: ACT is a third-wave therapy (Hayes) built on acceptance and mindfulness.
wrong.b: True: DBT is a third-wave therapy (Linehan) with core mindfulness skills.
wrong.c: True: MBCT is a third-wave therapy that joins mindfulness practice to cognitive therapy.

q: In Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), the "core mindfulness" skills are primarily derived from which tradition?

concept.t: Marsha Linehan drew DBT's core mindfulness skills from Zen practice.
She balanced this acceptance against cognitive-behavioural change strategies.

wrong.a: Influenced Ellis's REBT, not DBT's mindfulness module.
wrong.c: Unrelated to DBT's mindfulness module, which comes from Zen, not the analytic tradition.
wrong.d: Also unrelated to DBT's mindfulness module, which is a Zen practice, not existential philosophy.

q: What is the primary focus of Indian psychology?
who: Indian psychology: Samkhya, Yoga, Vedanta, Buddhism

concept.t: Indian psychology draws its concepts and methods from Samkhya, Yoga, Vedanta, Buddhism and related traditions.
So its focus is integrating these philosophical traditions with psychological concepts.

wrong.a: Describes imitative psychology in India, the opposite of Indian psychology.
wrong.b: Indian psychology is not meditation stripped of theory; its practices sit inside a philosophical framework.
wrong.c: Indian psychology is not mythology; its sources are philosophical schools.

q: Who is regarded as the pioneer of psychology in India, establishing the first Indian psychological laboratory?
who: Girindrashekhar Bose, father of Indian psychoanalysis

concept.t: Bose, father of Indian psychoanalysis and Sengupta's Calcutta colleague, is the only pioneer listed.
Strictly, the first laboratory was set up by N. N. Sengupta at Calcutta in 1915, and Sengupta is not among the options.
If Sengupta does appear in the options, choose him for the first laboratory.

wrong.a: Not credited with founding psychology in India or its first laboratory.
wrong.b: Mangal is a textbook author, not a pioneer.
wrong.d: A. K. Singh is a textbook author, not a pioneer.

q: Who is considered the father of Indian psychology?
who: Indian Psychology movement; likely K. Ramakrishna Rao (2008 Handbook)

concept.t: The key appears to intend a leader of the Indian Psychology movement, most plausibly K. Ramakrishna Rao.
He co-edited the Handbook of Indian Psychology (2008).
If the question meant modern scientific psychology in India, the answer would be (a) Sengupta.

wrong.a: The pioneer of modern scientific psychology in India; right if the question meant that, but not the keyed answer.
wrong.b: Kakar is a psychoanalyst, not the father of the field.
wrong.c: Misra is a contemporary scholar of indigenous psychology, not the father of the field.

q: The concept of the three gunas comes mainly from which school of Indian philosophy, alongside the Bhagavad Gita?
who: Samkhya school, with the Bhagavad Gita

concept.t: In Samkhya, prakriti is composed of three gunas: sattva, rajas and tamas.
The Gita builds its psychology of personality on these three gunas.

wrong.a: The school of logic, not of the gunas.
wrong.b: The school of materialism, not of the gunas.
wrong.d: The school of Vedic ritual and duty, not of the gunas.

q: In Samkhya dualism, the principle of pure consciousness, the passive witness, is Purusha. The three gunas belong to its counterpart, which is:

concept.t: Prakriti, primordial matter, is made of the three gunas.
It is the counterpart of Purusha, pure consciousness, in Samkhya dualism.

wrong.a: A Vedantic term for the self, not Purusha's counterpart.
wrong.c: A Vedantic term for ultimate reality, not Purusha's counterpart.
wrong.d: One of prakriti's products, not its counterpart.

q: Bavisha lost her job. Since then she is stressed, has stopped eating properly and cannot get herself to do anything. According to yogic philosophy, the main issue she is dealing with is:
who: Theory of the three gunas: tamas

concept.t: Withdrawal, loss of appetite and inability to act are the signature of tamas.
Tamas is the guna of inertia and dullness.
Rajas would show as restless over-activity.

wrong.a: The first limb of yoga (ethical restraints), not a mental state, so it cannot describe her condition.
wrong.c: Fails because yama is an ethical limb of yoga, not a mental state, so only tamas fits.
wrong.d: Would show as restless over-activity, the opposite of her withdrawal and inertia.

q: In Indian psychology, the 'inner instrument' (antahkarana) classically has four functions. Which one is the EGO or 'I-maker'?

concept.t: Ahamkara refers experience to a separate "I", which is why it is the ego or I-maker.
The antahkarana has four functions: manas, buddhi, ahamkara and chitta.

wrong.a: The sensory mind that doubts and deliberates, not the ego.
wrong.b: The intellect that decides, not the ego.
wrong.d: The store of memory impressions, not the ego.

q: According to Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, the primary goal of yoga is:

concept.t: Sutra 1.2 defines yoga as the stilling of the mind's fluctuations (citta vritti nirodha).
Its goal is kaivalya, consciousness resting in itself.

wrong.a: May be a by-product of practice, but it is not the goal.
wrong.c: Sharper cognition may be a by-product, but it is not the goal.
wrong.d: Calmer emotions may be a by-product, but they are not the goal, and "only" makes it narrower still.

q: Which is the correct order of the last four of Patanjali's eight limbs?
who: Patanjali's eight limbs, last four in order

concept.t: The senses must first be withdrawn (pratyahara) before attention can be fixed (dharana).
Fixed attention becomes an unbroken flow (dhyana), and the flow becomes absorption (samadhi).

wrong.a: Puts withdrawal after concentration; the senses must be withdrawn before attention can be fixed.
wrong.c: Swaps concentration and meditation: attention must be fixed (dharana) before it can flow (dhyana).
wrong.d: Swaps concentration and meditation and also puts withdrawal after concentration.

q: In the Pancha Kosha model, the five sheaths of the self run from gross to subtle. The OUTERMOST sheath, the physical body sustained by food, is:

concept.t: Anna means food, so annamaya kosha, the food sheath, is the gross body.
From outer to inner: annamaya, pranamaya, manomaya, vijnanamaya, anandamaya.

wrong.b: The vital sheath of breath, one layer inside the food sheath.
wrong.c: The mental sheath of perception and emotion, deeper than the body.
wrong.d: The innermost bliss sheath, the opposite end of the series.
